chunks: And if the divine favor (lutf) had not already passed from them, it is permissible for him to be concealed from them, even if it is conceded that what occurs is a favor for them. And with that, it was said: 'Why does he not appear to them?' We said: 'That is not obligatory in all circumstances,' so the question was invalidated from its root.

Moreover, their favor is in its place from another aspect, which is that because of his concealment, they trust in the arrival of all the Sharia to them. And if it were not for it, they would not trust in that, and it would be permissible for much of the Sharia to be hidden from them and cut off from them. And when they know his existence in general, they are secure from all that, so the favor is in its place from this aspect as well.

And we have mentioned previously that the concealment of the birth of the Master of the Age (peace be upon him) is not an extraordinary event breaking customs, as similar things have occurred in the narrations of kings that preceded. And the scholars of the Persians and those who narrated the news of the two dynasties have mentioned it.

Among that is what is well-known, such as the story of Kaykhusraw, and what was from the concealment of his mother's pregnancy and the hiding of his birth, and his mother was the daughter of Afrasiab, king of the Turks, and his grandfather Kaikawas wanted to kill his son, so his mother hid him until she gave birth to him, and there was from his story what is well-known in the books of histories, which Tabari mentioned.
ai.seo_question: Why is the concealment of the Imam considered a divine favor rather than a loss?
ai.summary: Al-Tusi resolves the theological objection that concealing the Imam's birth contradicts divine favor (lutf) by arguing that the very act of concealment guarantees the people's trust in the complete transmission of Sharia, thus serving as a distinct form of lutf. He grounds this in historical precedent, citing Persian monarchs like Kaykhusraw and the Sassanian era to demonstrate that hidden births are established customs (‘adah) rather than supernatural exceptions, thereby validating the Imam's occultation within the natural order.

en.sayyid-athar-husain-s-h-rizvi: We previously mentioned that the concealed birth of the Master of the Age is not extraordinary, as the likes of it have occurred in narrated stories of kings. Scholars of Persia and other biographers of rulers have mentioned similar accounts, such as the well-known story of Kaikhisrau;
whose mother was the daughter of Afrasyab, king of the Turks, and concealed his conception and birth, and whose grandfather, Kaikawas, the king of Persia, desired to kill him.
and his story is famous in history. Tabari has mentioned it in his Tarikh.
